description: We're a team of Computer Engineering students from Ankara University, united by a shared curiosity for technology. We joined the NASA Space Apps Challenge to apply our foundational Python skills to real problems. As friends and collaborative learners, our goal is to challenge ourselves, gain hands-on experience, and grow together as future software engineers.
summary:
MISSION CRITICAL is a browser-based (WebGL) space systems engineering and orbital flight simulator built in Unity. It makes complex mission architecture intuitive yet scientifically rigorous: players design end-to-end missions across NASA’s four core segments (Launch, Space, Ground, and User) using the Concept Maturity Level (CML 1–4) framework and real-time Red-Yellow-Green (RYG) margin checks.

Unlike simplified arcade space games, MISSION CRITICAL builds its physics on orbital parameters from NASA GMAT and JPL Horizons, using a Runge-Kutta 8(9) integrator, the JGM-2 gravity model and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, across a 3-mission campaign: Low Earth Orbit (LEO), Geostationary Orbit (GEO) and Lunar transfer. Players manage LEOP deployment, battery cycles through eclipses, and a solar-flare crisis dilemma, while an Auto-Fill assistant helps newcomers reach full readiness. With three difficulty tiers (Explorer, Standard, Engineer) and live English/Turkish switching, it brings real NASA systems engineering to high-school and university learners.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

MISSION CRITICAL is a web-accessible (Unity WebGL) interactive space mission design and orbital flight simulator grounded in NASA systems engineering methodologies. Players progress through a 3-mission sequential campaign, Low Earth Orbit (LEO, 550 km), Geostationary Orbit (GEO, 35,786 km), and Lunar Orbit (100 km, reached via Trans-Lunar Injection), following the Concept Maturity Level (CML 1–4) loop:

  1. CML 1–3 (4-Segment Hangar Trade Space): Players configure subsystems across the Launch, Space, Ground, and User segments (launch vehicles, spacecraft buses, solar arrays, batteries, transceivers, thermal kits, science instruments, ground stations, and data centers), or deploy a verified green baseline using the 100% Optimal Design Auto-Fill solver.
  2. CML 4 (Real-Time Point Design & RYG Verification): A 5-equation physics and engineering core evaluates Mass Margin (≥35% target), Power and Eclipse Energy Balance, RF Link Margin and Downlink Loss, Thermal Dissipation, and Budget Reserve (+20% margin), displaying results as Red-Yellow-Green (RYG) status indicators.
  3. LEOP & Orbital Operations: Once launch-ready, players execute multi-day Launch and Early Orbit Phase (LEOP) milestones: ascent to a 185 km parking orbit, booster separation with immediate solar array deployment, spiral orbit raising, and ground beacon lock. They then manage real-time eclipse battery integration (Wh), solar storm (CME) mitigation, and spacecraft load-shedding decisions.
  4. Post-Mission Debrief: Science yield is scored using the QQCL framework of Wessen et al. (Quantity, Quality, Continuity, Latency), alongside automated root-cause failure analysis and analogous NASA mission class matching (Levri, 2025: PUNCH, PILOT, Dawn, and Mars Moon Sampler).

Tools, Software & Data Used

  • Game Engine & Language: Unity 6 (C#), TextMeshPro, and Unity WebGL (deployed on Unity Play).
  • Orbital Mechanics & NASA Data: Orbital parameters (altitude, velocity, period, eclipse fraction, and transfer Δv) derived from NASA GMAT (General Mission Analysis Tool) and JPL Horizons. The simulation engine uses Runge-Kutta 8(9) numerical propagation, the JGM-2 gravity field model, and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for fuel and mass calculations.
  • Procedural Graphics & Audio: Custom C# runtime procedural texture synthesis (Texture2D for Earth and Moon terrain, terminator shading, and solar flux gradients) and procedural WebGL audio synthesis (AudioClip), ensuring zero external asset dependencies and instant browser loading.

Intended Impact, Creativity & Design Factors

Professional astrodynamics tools such as NASA GMAT demand deep technical expertise, while arcade space games leave out real engineering trade-offs. MISSION CRITICAL bridges this gap by building its physics on GMAT- and JPL Horizons-derived parameters and wrapping them in three tailored difficulty tiers: Explorer Mode guided by Commander Nova, Standard Mode, and Engineer Mode with live radiator cooling and Δv station-keeping burns. Live English/Turkish localization makes the experience accessible beyond a single language community. The game gives high-school and university students, educators, and aspiring aerospace engineers a hands-on way to experience real NASA systems engineering, from early concept design to crisis management after launch.
